\chapter{Noon and Midnight}
\label{ch:spanish-noon-midnight}
\hlchaptermodality{63}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that it is noon or midnight in Spanish and break both words into their two living halves.}

Say es mediodía and es medianoche, split each into medio/media plus día/noche, and set them against French's worn-down midi and minuit.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mediodía, medianoche]{mediodía, medianoche — noon and midnight, spelled out in full}

\label{lesson:ES-C28-mediodia-medianoche}



\begin{quote}
Two hours that don't get a number — they get a name. And Spanish keeps that name far more transparent than its French cousin does.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{$\leftarrow$ Latin} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{mediodía} & \emph{medius diēs} & \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{mid}-\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{medio} \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{} + \emph{día} \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}) \\
\textbf{medianoche} & \emph{media nox} & \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{mid}-\textbf{night}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{media} \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{} + \emph{noche} \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both halves are \textbf{fully alive, ordinary Spanish words on their own}: \textbf{medio/media} (\textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{} — cousin of English \emph{medium, mid, middle}) and \textbf{día/noche} (\textquotedblleft{}day/night,\textquotedblright{} words you already know). Compare French, which took the same Latin phrase down a bumpier road: \emph{minuit}'s second half, \textbf{-nuit}, is still the plain, everyday French word for \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} — just as recognizable as Spanish's \emph{noche}. But \emph{midi}'s second half, \textbf{-di}, wore down into an opaque fragment: the ordinary French word for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} is \emph{jour}, not \emph{di} — that piece survives only as a fossil, tucked inside weekday names like \emph{lundi} and \emph{mardi}. So the erosion split unevenly: French kept \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} transparent and lost \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} while Spanish kept both.

They don't need \emph{horas} the way a normal Spanish time (\emph{son las tres}) never does either — they simply stand in for the hour on their own:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Es mediodía.} — \textquotedblleft{}It is noon.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Es medianoche.} — \textquotedblleft{}It is midnight.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

(Fun aside: English \textbf{noon} comes from Latin \emph{nōna hōra}, \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{ninth} hour\textquotedblright{} — originally mid-afternoon, it drifted earlier over the centuries to mean midday. Spanish kept the tidier, transparent \textquotedblleft{}mid-day\textquotedblright{} instead.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mediodía\textquotedblright{} (noon), \textquotedblleft{}medianoche\textquotedblright{} (midnight)
  \item break them — \textquotedblleft{}medio + día\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}media + noche\textquotedblright{} — both halves still ordinary words
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Es mediodía. Es medianoche.\textquotedblright{} — they stand in for the hour
  \item the contrast — French kept \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} (nuit) but wore \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} down to a fossil (-di)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \emph{mediodía} and \emph{medianoche} literally mean, and from what Latin? (\textquotedblleft{}Mid-day\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{medius diēs}; \textquotedblleft{}mid-night\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{media nox}.) Are both halves still recognizable, ordinary Spanish words? (\textbf{Yes} — \emph{medio/ media} \textquotedblleft{}middle,\textquotedblright{} \emph{día/noche} \textquotedblleft{}day/night.\textquotedblright{}) Did French erode its phrase evenly? (\textbf{No} — French's \emph{-nuit} stayed just as transparent as Spanish's \emph{noche}, but its \emph{-di} wore down to an opaque fossil, since the everyday French word for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} is actually \emph{jour}.) How do you say \textquotedblleft{}it is noon\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Es mediodía}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
